def: A genus of flagellated protozoa. T. vaginalis is a sexually transmitted parasite causing frothy green vaginal discharge and a "strawberry" cervix; motile trophozoites are seen on wet mount and treated with metronidazole.
A benzimidazole antihelminthic that binds worm beta-tubulin and blocks microtubule assembly. Used for neurocysticercosis, hydatid cysts, and roundworm and hookworm infections.
Soft, cauliflower-like warts of the genital and anal skin, caused by HPV types 6 and 11 and spread sexually. Biopsy shows koilocytes (cells with a clear halo around a wrinkled nucleus).

An antibiotic that inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase, blocking tetrahydrofolate synthesis. Usually combined with sulfamethoxazole for urinary infections and Pneumocystis; can cause hyperkalemia and megaloblastic anemia.

Sterile joint inflammation that follows a gut or genital infection (Chlamydia, Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter). Classic triad is arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis; associated with HLA-B27.
Large binucleate or multinucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli, derived from B cells. Their presence is diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma; they are CD15 and CD30 positive.
A genus of thin, corkscrew-shaped spirochetes that stain poorly with Gram stain and are seen by darkfield microscopy. T. pallidum causes syphilis.
An atypical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Notable for hyperprolactinemia, weight gain and extrapyramidal side effects.
A gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas or duodenum. Excess gastrin causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome: severe, recurrent peptic ulcers and diarrhea; associated with MEN1.

An indolent B-cell leukemia with cells bearing hair-like cytoplasmic projections that stain TRAP positive, carrying a BRAF V600E mutation. Causes pancytopenia and splenomegaly with a dry marrow tap; treated with cladribine.
Rapid NADPH oxidase-driven production of superoxide and other reactive oxygen species by phagocytes to kill engulfed microbes. It is defective in chronic granulomatous disease.
The membrane enzyme that converts ATP to cyclic AMP. It is stimulated by Gs-coupled receptors and inhibited by Gi-coupled receptors.
A 20-carbon omega-6 fatty acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. It is the precursor of prostaglandins and thromboxanes (cyclooxygenase) and leukotrienes (lipoxygenase).
A receptor tyrosine kinase that autophosphorylates when insulin binds. It signals through IRS-1 and PI3K/Akt to move GLUT4 to the cell surface, and through MAP kinase to promote growth.
Drugs that activate dopamine receptors, such as bromocriptine, cabergoline, pramipexole and ropinirole. Used for Parkinson disease, restless legs syndrome and prolactinomas.

A peptide hormone made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It acts on V2 receptors to insert aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct (water retention) and on V1 receptors to constrict vessels.

A hormonal cascade in which kidney renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and ACE converts that to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone, raising blood pressure and sodium retention.
Low serum albumin, caused by nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition or inflammation. It lowers plasma oncotic pressure and so causes edema.
An adipocyte enzyme that hydrolyzes stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol. It is activated by epinephrine and glucagon (via PKA) and inhibited by insulin.
A 46,XY disorder caused by a defective androgen receptor. Patients have testes and female external genitalia, a blind vagina, no uterus, and high testosterone and LH.
Skin glands attached to hair follicles that secrete oily sebum. Androgens stimulate them, and their plugging and inflammation underlie acne.
An intracellular nuclear receptor that binds estradiol and acts as a transcription factor. Estrogen receptor positivity in breast cancer predicts response to tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors.
Secretion of the cervix that becomes thin, watery and stretchy under estrogen near ovulation (dries in a ferning pattern) and thick under progesterone.
The second half of the menstrual cycle, after ovulation, in which the corpus luteum secretes progesterone to prepare the endometrium. It lasts a fairly constant 14 days.
A prenatal procedure in which a needle is passed through the abdomen to sample amniotic fluid, usually at 15-20 weeks. Used for karyotype, alpha-fetoprotein and fetal lung maturity.
An essential branched-chain amino acid. Its accumulation with leucine and isoleucine occurs in maple syrup urine disease, and a glutamate-to-valine substitution causes sickle cell hemoglobin.
Hair-like microtubule projections from the cell surface. Motile cilia (9+2 arrangement, dynein arms) move mucus and fluid; defective dynein causes primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome).
An inherited defect in type I collagen synthesis causing fragile bones with frequent fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Small circular DNA molecules in bacteria that replicate independently of the chromosome. They often carry antibiotic resistance or virulence genes and spread by conjugation.
A technique in which fluorescently labeled cells pass single file past a laser, allowing counting and sorting by surface markers (CD antigens). Used to diagnose leukemias, lymphomas and PNH.

A malignant small round blue cell tumor of bone in children and young adults, typically the diaphysis of long bones, with onion-skin periosteal reaction. Carries t(11;22) producing the EWS-FLI1 fusion.
An inherited lack of melanin production (often tyrosinase deficiency) with a normal number of melanocytes. Causes pale skin and hair, vision problems and a higher risk of skin cancer.

A focal outpouching of a cerebral artery, most often a berry aneurysm at a branch point of the circle of Willis. Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage; associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

A rapid negative feedback loop in which stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense blood pressure. Falling pressure reduces firing to the nucleus solitarius, increasing sympathetic output and heart rate.
Tissue rich in lymphocytes where immune responses are organized, including lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

Delivery of a synchronized electrical shock to the heart to convert an abnormal rhythm, such as atrial fibrillation or unstable ventricular tachycardia, to sinus rhythm. Unsynchronized shocks are defibrillation.

An inflammatory condition of older adults with aching and morning stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles, a high ESR, and dramatic response to low-dose steroids. Associated with giant cell arteritis.
Black, tarry, foul-smelling stool from digested blood, signaling bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract.
The uppermost part of the pharynx, behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Contains the adenoids and eustachian tube openings; site of EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, usually from thrombosis, causing painful hepatomegaly, ascites and centrilobular congestion. Associated with polycythemia vera and other hypercoagulable states.
A class IA antiarrhythmic that blocks sodium and potassium channels, prolonging the QT interval. Can cause torsades de pointes and cinchonism (tinnitus, headache); also an antimalarial.
Listening to sounds from the heart, lungs or abdomen, usually with a stethoscope.
Impaired pumping (systolic, with reduced ejection fraction) or impaired filling (diastolic) of the left ventricle, leading to heart failure.
Viable bacteria in the bloodstream, which may be transient (after dental work) or may progress to sepsis.
An anthracycline chemotherapy drug that intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II. Used in acute myeloid leukemia; causes dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy.
Elevated arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO2 above about 45 mmHg), from hypoventilation. Causes respiratory acidosis, cerebral vasodilation and drowsiness.
Severe one-sided pain around the eye lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, in clusters, with ipsilateral tearing, nasal congestion and Horner features. Treated with oxygen and triptans.
Cells such as neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages that engulf and digest microbes and debris.
A genus of Gram-negative diplococci. M. catarrhalis causes otitis media, sinusitis and COPD exacerbations, and produces beta-lactamase.
Antibodies or lectins that clump cells such as red cells or bacteria. Cold agglutinins (IgM) cause hemolysis after Mycoplasma pneumoniae or mononucleosis.
Inflammation of the parotid gland. Mumps virus is the classic cause; bacterial parotitis (S. aureus) occurs with dehydration or duct stones.
The fat and connective tissue layer beneath the dermis, which insulates and cushions. Also called the hypodermis.
The triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Classically follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 diarrhea in children.
An E. coli strain producing Shiga-like toxin, causing bloody diarrhea and hemolytic-uremic syndrome. O157:H7 is sorbitol-negative; acquired from undercooked beef.
Removal of a patient's plasma and replacement with fluid or albumin, clearing antibodies or toxins. Used in Guillain-Barre syndrome, myasthenic crisis, TTP and Goodpasture syndrome.
Myoglobin in the urine from muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), causing dark urine that is dipstick-positive for blood without red cells. Risks acute kidney injury.
An oral direct factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulant used for DVT, pulmonary embolism and atrial fibrillation. Needs no routine monitoring; reversed by andexanet alfa.
Deep swelling of the lower dermis and submucosa (lips, tongue, larynx) mediated by histamine or bradykinin. Caused by ACE inhibitors or hereditary C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency.
The cascade of serum proteins (classical, alternative, lectin pathways) converging on C3 cleavage. Yields opsonization (C3b), inflammation (C3a, C5a) and the membrane attack complex.
Hard stones formed from minerals or crystals in hollow organs, such as kidney stones and gallstones.
Clonal bone marrow neoplasms with overproduction of mature blood cells: polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis and CML. The first three often carry JAK2 mutations.
Drugs that bind metal ions to promote their excretion in poisoning, such as EDTA, dimercaprol, succimer, deferoxamine and penicillamine.
An inherited failure of osteoclast bone resorption causing dense, brittle bones, marrow crowding with pancytopenia, and cranial nerve compression.
The main ketone body, made from acetoacetate in the liver; it rises in diabetic ketoacidosis and starvation and is not detected by the nitroprusside urine test.
Severe, persistent vomiting in early pregnancy with weight loss, dehydration and ketonuria. Linked to high hCG, as in molar pregnancy and twins.
Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency causing dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia, with a rash on sun-exposed skin. Seen in Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome and isoniazid use.
A fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes from lipid peroxidation. Deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, spinocerebellar ataxia and neuropathy.
An anticholinergic (muscarinic antagonist) used for parkinsonism and drug-induced extrapyramidal symptoms. Side effects include dry mouth, urinary retention and confusion.
A malignancy of myeloid blasts in the marrow, with Auer rods on smear. The promyelocytic subtype carries t(15;17) and is treated with all-trans retinoic acid.
A myeloproliferative neoplasm in which marrow fibrosis causes teardrop red cells, a dry marrow tap, and extramedullary hematopoiesis with massive splenomegaly. Often JAK2 mutated.
A benign Schwann cell tumor of cranial nerve VIII at the cerebellopontine angle, causing hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. Bilateral tumors suggest neurofibromatosis type 2.
A malignant small blue cell tumor of the cerebellum in children, with Homer Wright rosettes. Arises in the vermis and obstructs the fourth ventricle, causing hydrocephalus.
A glioma arising from ependymal cells lining the ventricles. In children it usually occurs in the fourth ventricle and causes hydrocephalus; histology shows perivascular pseudorosettes.
The posterior cerebral lobe that holds the primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus. Lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
Inflammation of lymph nodes, making them tender and swollen, usually from infection in the area they drain.
Abnormal pain or discomfort from light, seen in meningitis, migraine and uveitis.
Diseases of the white matter of the brain, such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and toxic leukoencephalopathy.

Dementia with alpha-synuclein inclusions (Lewy bodies), featuring fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behavior disorder, with severe sensitivity to antipsychotics.
Enlarged ventricles with normal CSF pressure in older adults, causing gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia. Often improves after CSF removal or shunting.

An eating disorder of binge eating followed by compensatory purging (vomiting, laxatives) with normal body weight. Complications include dental erosion, Russell sign, parotid enlargement and hypokalemia.
Vomiting of blood, indicating upper gastrointestinal bleeding such as from varices or an ulcer.
Free air in the peritoneal cavity, seen as air under the diaphragm on an upright x-ray. Signals a perforated hollow organ, or follows laparoscopy.
A benign bone tumor, commonly of the skull and facial bones. Multiple osteomas suggest Gardner syndrome.
An adenocarcinoma of the bile duct epithelium that presents with painless jaundice. Risks include primary sclerosing cholangitis and liver flukes (Clonorchis).
Nutrition delivered directly into a vein, bypassing the gut. Complications include line infection, hyperglycemia, cholestasis and refeeding syndrome.
The duct formed by the cystic and common hepatic ducts that carries bile to the duodenum, joining the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater. A stone here causes obstructive jaundice.
A short-acting benzodiazepine that increases the frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening. Used for procedural sedation and status epilepticus; reversed by flumazenil.
A severe fall in neutrophils (below about 500/uL) that leaves patients prone to infection. Caused by clozapine, carbamazepine, propylthiouracil, methimazole and sulfonamides.
An observational study comparing past exposures in people with a disease (cases) to those without (controls). Yields an odds ratio and suits rare diseases.
Treatment with light. In neonates, blue light converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers that are excreted without conjugation; UVB treats psoriasis.
Cell-surface receptors, commonly receptor tyrosine kinases (EGFR, VEGFR, PDGFR), that drive proliferation when bound by growth factors. Mutations or overexpression are oncogenic.
A genus of Gram-negative coccobacilli. P. multocida from cat and dog bites causes rapid-onset cellulitis; treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate.
A tapeworm genus. E. granulosus (from dogs, sheep) forms hydatid cysts in liver and lung; cyst spillage can cause anaphylaxis. Treated with albendazole and surgery.
An antifungal that inhibits squalene epoxidase, blocking ergosterol synthesis. Used orally for onychomycosis and dermatophyte infections; can cause hepatotoxicity.
Antifungals (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) that inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthase in the fungal cell wall. Given intravenously for invasive Candida and Aspergillus.
Pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila from contaminated water (air conditioning, showers), with high fever, diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia. Diagnosed by urine antigen.
Viruses transmitted by arthropods such as mosquitoes and ticks, including dengue, yellow fever, West Nile, Zika and eastern equine encephalitis viruses.
Seizures triggered by fever in children aged about 6 months to 5 years without CNS infection. Usually brief and generalized, with a benign course.
A protozoan genus spread by sandflies, with amastigotes living in macrophages. Causes cutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral (kala-azar) disease; treated with sodium stibogluconate.
Sampling tissue with a needle, either fine-needle aspiration for cells or core biopsy for a tissue cylinder.
A congenital hole in the wall between the atria, most often ostium secundum. Causes a left-to-right shunt with fixed splitting of S2 and risk of paradoxical embolism.
Bacterial toxins that act on the intestine to cause diarrhea or vomiting, such as cholera toxin, ETEC toxins and preformed Staphylococcus aureus toxin in food poisoning.
Infection with Trypanosoma cruzi spread by reduviid (kissing bug) feces. The chronic phase causes dilated cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus and megacolon.
An elevated absolute lymphocyte count, seen in viral infections (EBV, pertussis) and chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
The spirochete that causes syphilis. It cannot be cultured and is seen by darkfield microscopy; diagnosed by RPR/VDRL then FTA-ABS, and treated with penicillin G.
An antibiotic that binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks tRNA attachment. Used for Rickettsia, Borrelia, Chlamydia and acne; avoided in pregnancy and children, and chelated by calcium and iron.
Enzymes that transfer a functional group from one molecule to another, such as kinases and aminotransferases.
An enzyme that phosphorylates thymidine in nucleotide salvage. Viral thymidine kinase activates acyclovir by the first phosphorylation.

An antiviral pyrophosphate analog that directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase without needing activation by viral kinases. Used for CMV and acyclovir-resistant HSV; causes nephrotoxicity and electrolyte loss.
Minimally invasive abdominal surgery or inspection using a camera and instruments passed through small incisions.
A medullary nucleus that receives visceral afferents, including taste (CN VII, IX, X), baroreceptors and chemoreceptors.

A life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics) with fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability and high CK. Treated with dantrolene or bromocriptine.
A long-acting somatostatin analog used for carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma, acromegaly and variceal bleeding. Can cause gallstones.
A sugar alcohol made from glucose by aldose reductase. It accumulates in the lens, nerves and retina in diabetes, contributing to cataracts and neuropathy.
A nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor used for HIV and hepatitis B. Can cause kidney injury (Fanconi syndrome) and loss of bone density.
An essential amino acid with a hydroxyl group. It is a site of phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases and of O-linked glycosylation.
Transmembrane receptors, including insulin, EGF, VEGF and PDGF receptors, that dimerize and autophosphorylate tyrosines on ligand binding, activating Ras/MAPK and PI3K pathways.
Deficient ADH from hypothalamic or posterior pituitary damage (trauma, tumor), causing large volumes of dilute urine and thirst. Urine concentrates after desmopressin.
A weak androgen made by the adrenal zona reticularis and a precursor of testosterone and estrogen. Its sulfate (DHEAS) is a marker of adrenal androgen production.
A pancreatic beta-cell tumor secreting insulin, causing fasting hypoglycemia with high C-peptide. Associated with MEN1.
A peptide from parathyroid chief cells that raises serum calcium (bone resorption, renal reabsorption, activation of vitamin D) and lowers phosphate.
Severe hypothyroidism with non-pitting skin swelling from glycosaminoglycan deposition. Myxedema coma is its life-threatening extreme.
A painful thyroid inflammation after a viral illness, with granulomas, high ESR, transient thyrotoxicosis then hypothyroidism, and low radioiodine uptake.
A thyroid cancer of follicular cells that spreads through blood to bone and lung. Diagnosis requires capsular or vascular invasion, not just cytology.
An enzyme that removes a carboxyl group as CO2, often using pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6), as in DOPA decarboxylase and glutamate decarboxylase.
The muscular tube that carries sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct, cut in vasectomy. It derives from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct.
Seals between neighboring epithelial cells (claudins, occludin) that block paracellular leak and keep apical and basolateral membrane proteins separate.
Whip-like appendages for motility. Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin and rotate; sperm flagella have a 9+2 microtubule core.
A weak estrogen (E1) that predominates after menopause, made in fat tissue from androstenedione by aromatase.
A synthetic progestin used for emergency contraception, pills and intrauterine devices. It acts mainly by delaying ovulation.
An aggressive testicular germ cell tumor with hemorrhagic, necrotic glandular or papillary growth. Positive for CD30 and cytokeratin; may raise hCG and AFP.
New-onset seizures in a pregnant woman with preeclampsia (hypertension and proteinuria). Treated with magnesium sulfate and delivery.
The 47,XXY karyotype in males: tall stature, small firm testes, gynecomastia and infertility from hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. A Barr body is present.
Cancer staging by primary Tumor size, regional lymph Node involvement and distant Metastasis.
Calcium-dependent adhesion molecules at adherens junctions. Loss of E-cadherin lets tumor cells detach and invade, as in lobular breast and diffuse gastric cancer.
Death of bone from loss of blood supply (avascular necrosis), classically the femoral head. Causes include steroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease and trauma.
Involuntary urination in a child past the age of expected bladder control, usually about 5 years.
Involuntary urination during sleep in a child old enough to be continent. Usually benign and resolves with age; treated with alarms or desmopressin.
Failure of the uterus to contract after delivery, the commonest cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Treated with uterine massage, oxytocin and methylergonovine.
Inactive compounds converted in the body to the active drug, such as levodopa, enalapril, codeine and azathioprine.
Enzymes that cleave nucleotides one at a time from the end of a nucleic acid. The 3'-to-5' activity of DNA polymerase proofreads, and 5'-to-3' activity removes RNA primers.
Autosomal recessive loss of anterior horn motor neurons from SMN1 deletion, causing a floppy infant with weakness and tongue fasciculations (Werdnig-Hoffmann disease).
Thin polymers of actin that form the cytoskeleton, support microvilli and cell shape, and drive muscle contraction and cell movement.
Muscular projections inside the ventricles that anchor chordae tendineae to valve leaflets. Rupture after myocardial infarction causes acute mitral regurgitation.
Increased blood flow to a tissue, active (exercise, inflammation) or reactive (after temporary occlusion), causing redness and warmth. Distinct from congestion, which is impaired venous outflow.
Narrowing of the internal carotid artery by atherosclerosis. A source of emboli causing TIA, stroke or amaurosis fugax; treated with endarterectomy.
The commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide, with mesangial IgA deposits. Causes recurrent hematuria 1-3 days after an upper respiratory or gut infection.
A lipid-rich lesion in the arterial intima with a fibrous cap and necrotic core containing foam cells. Rupture triggers thrombosis, causing infarction.
A liver hormone that lowers iron availability by degrading ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages. Raised in anemia of chronic disease.
A beta-1 agonist that increases cardiac contractility. Used in acute decompensated heart failure and for pharmacologic stress testing.
A large structural protein of VLDL, IDL and LDL made by the liver, and the ligand for the LDL receptor. Defects cause familial hypercholesterolemia.
Opposition to airflow in the airways, proportional to 1/radius^4. Greatest in medium-sized bronchi, and raised in asthma and COPD.
IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal lining to allergens, causing sneezing, itching and watery discharge, with pale boggy turbinates.
The canal connecting the middle ear to the nasopharynx, equalizing pressure. It is short and horizontal in children, predisposing to otitis media.
An encapsulated Gram-negative lactose-fermenting rod with mucoid colonies. Causes pneumonia in alcoholics (currant jelly sputum), urinary infection and liver abscess.
Progressive scarring of the lungs of unknown cause in older adults, with dry crackles, clubbing and honeycombing on CT. Histology shows usual interstitial pneumonia.
A large extracellular matrix glycoprotein binding integrins, collagen and fibrin to mediate cell adhesion and wound healing. Fetal fibronectin predicts preterm delivery.
The enzyme that phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, trapping it in the cell. It has a low Km and is inhibited by its product, unlike liver glucokinase.
Inherited enzyme defects of glycogen synthesis or breakdown, causing glycogen buildup in liver or muscle, with hypoglycemia or exercise intolerance depending on type.
Glycogen storage disease type I, from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. Causes severe fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia.
Enzymes that hydrolyze ester bonds, such as acetylcholinesterase and lipases. Leukocyte esterase on urinalysis suggests pus in the urine.
An inhaled muscarinic antagonist bronchodilator used in COPD and asthma exacerbations. Causes dry mouth.
Inadequate digestive enzyme secretion by the pancreas, as in chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis, causing fatty stools and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Treated with enzyme replacement.
The filtration layer between glomerular endothelium and podocytes, made of type IV collagen and negatively charged heparan sulfate. Damaged in Alport syndrome and anti-GBM disease.
Autosomal recessive loss of the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal tubule, causing hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia and low urine calcium.
Backward flow of urine from the bladder up the ureters, from an incompetent ureterovesical junction. Predisposes children to pyelonephritis and renal scarring.
Enzyme complexes of the complement system that cleave C3 into C3a and C3b (C4b2a or C3bBb). Adding another C3b yields C5 convertase, which cleaves C5 to start the membrane attack complex.
The dimer of two cysteines joined by a disulfide bond. In cystinuria it forms hexagonal stones from defective renal reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine.
A mitochondrial urea cycle enzyme forming citrulline from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate. X-linked deficiency causes hyperammonemia with high orotic acid.
A prodrug of mycophenolic acid that inhibits IMPDH, blocking de novo guanine synthesis in lymphocytes. An immunosuppressant for transplant and lupus nephritis; teratogenic.
A chronic greasy, flaky red rash of the scalp, face and nasolabial folds, linked to Malassezia yeast. More common in Parkinson disease and HIV.
Abnormal fluid in two or more fetal compartments (ascites, pleural effusion, edema). Immune causes include Rh disease; nonimmune include alpha-thalassemia major and parvovirus B19.
Multipotent CD34-positive marrow cells that self-renew and give rise to all blood cell lineages. Basis of bone marrow transplantation.
A urinary antiseptic for uncomplicated urinary infections that damages bacterial DNA. Avoided in renal impairment; can cause pulmonary fibrosis and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
The embryonic hindbrain division that gives rise to the pons and cerebellum.
Non-neuronal supporting cells of the nervous system: astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells and Schwann cells.
Cranial nerve IX: taste from the posterior third of the tongue, pharyngeal sensation (afferent limb of the gag reflex), carotid sinus input, and motor supply to stylopharyngeus and parotid secretion.
Inflammation of a nerve causing pain, sensory loss or weakness, as in optic neuritis.
Staining tissue sections with labeled antibodies to detect specific proteins. Used to classify tumors, for example with cytokeratin, S100 or CD markers.
A branch of the internal carotid supplying the medial frontal and parietal lobes. Stroke causes contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, and abulia.
Inability to perform learned purposeful movements despite intact strength, sensation and comprehension, from parietal or frontal cortical lesions.
A DNA virus that mainly causes genital herpes and neonatal herpes, and lies latent in sacral ganglia. Multinucleated giant cells appear on Tzanck smear.
Sudden, brief, shock-like involuntary muscle jerks, seen in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, metabolic encephalopathy and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
A demyelinating brain disease from JC virus reactivation in immunosuppressed patients (AIDS, natalizumab), destroying oligodendrocytes and causing multifocal white matter lesions.
White plaques on the oral mucosa that scrape off, caused by Candida albicans. Seen in infants, inhaled steroid use, HIV and diabetes.
Dilated submucosal veins of the lower esophagus from portal hypertension, via the left gastric-azygos anastomosis. Rupture causes massive upper GI bleeding.
Air trapped under the skin that crackles on palpation, from pneumothorax, ruptured airway or esophagus, or gas-forming infection.
Measurement of pressure within a hollow organ, such as esophageal manometry showing incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation in achalasia.
Chronic itchy eczema in people with atopy, on the face and extensors in infants and the flexures in adults. Linked to filaggrin mutations, asthma and allergic rhinitis.
The left gastric artery (from the celiac trunk) and right gastric artery (from the hepatic artery) supply the lesser curvature of the stomach. The left gastric also feeds the lower esophagus.
Imaging that uses an injected radioactive tracer detected by a gamma camera, as in bone scans, V/Q scans and HIDA scans.
Lymphoid follicle aggregates in the ileal submucosa with M cells that sample antigens and B cells that class-switch to IgA.
Failure of intestinal peristalsis without mechanical blockage, from surgery, opioids or electrolyte disturbance (low potassium), causing distension and absent bowel sounds.
Psychotherapy that applies learning principles, such as exposure or systematic desensitization, to change maladaptive behavior.
Viruses that infect bacteria. They mediate transduction, carrying toxin genes for diphtheria, cholera, botulinum and Shiga toxins.
Bacteria with a thick peptidoglycan wall and teichoic acids and no outer membrane, retaining crystal violet and staining purple.
Heart muscle damage caused by drugs or toxins, such as doxorubicin (dilated cardiomyopathy), trastuzumab and cocaine.
An atypical antipsychotic blocking dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Notable for weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia and sedation.
A gabapentinoid binding the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. Used for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia and partial seizures; causes sedation and edema.
A bone fracture from repetitive loading, common in the metatarsals and tibia of runners and recruits. Radiographs are often normal early; bone scan or MRI detects it.
An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that does not enter the CNS. Treats myasthenia gravis; cholinergic side effects include diarrhea and bradycardia.
Fat accumulation in hepatocytes without heavy alcohol use, linked to obesity and insulin resistance. It can progress to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis.
The paired vertical anterior abdominal wall muscle enclosed in the rectus sheath, crossed by tendinous intersections. Flexes the trunk.
The immediate, nonspecific first-line defense without memory, comprising barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement and Toll-like receptors.
